title: Ideal Timing and the Speed-up Formula
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Stages, Timing and Speed-up
quickIdea: With n instructions, k stages, one clock per stage and no stalls, the pipeline takes (k + n - 1) cycles where the unpipelined machine takes n x k, so the speed-up is nk / (k + n - 1), which climbs towards k as n grows.
remember: Pipelined time T = (k + n - 1) t_p; unpipelined time T = n k t_p, with the same clock period in both.
Speed-up S = nk / (k + n - 1). As n tends to infinity S tends to k, so k is the ceiling and no finite program reaches it.
Efficiency = S / k = n / (k + n - 1); throughput in the steady state = 1 / t_p instructions per cycle.
The formula assumes balanced stages, no stalls and the same clock in both designs. Break any one of the three and the diagram or the CPI equation must take over.
For a short program the fill dominates: 8 instructions on 5 stages give 12 cycles, so S = 40/12 = 3.33, not 5.

example.prompt: A five-stage pipeline has stage delays 150, 120, 150, 160 and 140 ns and inter-stage registers of 5 ns each. What is the total time for 100 independent instructions with no stalls?
example.work: t_p = max(150, 120, 150, 160, 140) + 5 = 160 + 5 = 165 ns. Cycles = k + n - 1 = 5 + 100 - 1 = 104. Time = 104 x 165 = 17160 ns. The unpipelined machine at the same clock would need 100 x 5 x 165 = 82500 ns, so the realised speed-up is 82500/17160 = 4.81 against a ceiling of 5.
example.answer: 17160 ns, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q.53, with a realised speed-up of 4.81.

gateAngle: The exam rarely asks for the formula; it asks for a number that the formula or the diagram produces. Where the program is short, or a stage is variable, the formula is the wrong tool and the diagram is the right one - GATE CSE 2018 Q.50 is the case in point, where (k + n - 1) alone gives 104 and the answer is 219.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For the 2021 Set 1 pipeline above, how many instructions must run before the realised speed-up exceeds 4.9?
variations.why: It forces the formula to be solved for n instead of evaluated, which is the step candidates skip.
variations.answer: S = 5n/(5 + n - 1) = 5n/(n + 4) > 4.9 means 5n > 4.9n + 19.6, so 0.1n > 19.6 and n > 196. At n = 197 the speed-up is 985/201 = 4.90; the ceiling of 5 is never reached.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is the speed-up nk/(k + n - 1) always less than k, and when does it equal k?
variations.why: It tests whether the student knows the formula is a limit statement rather than an identity.
variations.answer: Because the numerator counts n k stage-slots of work while the denominator includes the k - 1 cycles of fill that produce no completed instruction. The two are equal only in the limit n tends to infinity, so k is a supremum, not an attainable value.

trap.what: Using nk/(k + n - 1) when the pipelined design runs at a different clock from the unpipelined one.
trap.why: The formula cancels the clock period on the assumption that it is the same in both designs. When pipelining costs frequency - as it nearly always does - the clock ratio must be carried into the calculation.
trap.counterexample: A 5-stage pipeline at 2 GHz against a non-pipelined machine at 2.5 GHz with CPI 5: the CPI ratio 5/1 suggests 5, but the true speed-up is (5/2.5)/(1/2) = 2/0.5 = 4, because the pipelined clock is slower.

check.question: A 10-stage pipeline runs a program of 90 instructions with no stalls. What is the speed-up over the unpipelined machine at the same clock, and what is the efficiency?
check.explanation: Cycles = 10 + 90 - 1 = 99, unpipelined work = 90 x 10 = 900 stage-slots, so S = 900/99 = 9.09; dividing by k gives the fraction of the ideal gain realised.
